client: I’ve been feeling so anxious about the family reunion next month. My cousin always makes these snide comments about my career choices in front of everyone, and it makes me feel small and embarrassed. I’m not even sure if therapy can help with something like this—it feels like it’s just the way they are.
therapist: It sounds like this situation with your cousin brings up a lot of worry and frustration, and I can hear how deeply it’s affecting you. Let’s explore how we can work together to reframe those moments and help you feel more confident in responding to those comments—it’s not just about changing them, but also about how you can empower yourself in those interactions.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I guess I just don’t see how reframing will change anything. My cousin is always so smug when they make those comments, and I feel like no matter what I do, they’ll just keep doing it. It’s hard to feel confident when I’m already dreading the whole event.
therapist: It sounds like you’re feeling defeated and overwhelmed by the idea of facing your cousin again, and I can hear the frustration and worry in your voice as you talk about it. While it’s true we can’t control their behavior, we can work on building your confidence and finding ways to respond that feel empowering to you—even if their comments don’t change. Let’s focus on what’s within your control and how you can feel more grounded in those moments.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I get what you’re saying about focusing on what’s within my control, but it still feels like no matter what I do, they’ll find a way to make me feel small. I guess I’m just worried that if I try to stand up to them, it’ll make things worse or create more tension in the family. It’s hard to feel empowered when I’m already anticipating failure.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of fear and hesitation about standing up to your cousin, and I can hear how overwhelming it feels when you think about the potential consequences. Your worry about creating tension or making things worse is completely valid, but let’s explore small, manageable steps you can take to assert yourself in a way that feels safe and true to you. Even small shifts in how you respond can help you feel more in control and less at the mercy of their comments.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess small steps sound better than trying to do something big, but I’m still not sure what those steps would even look like. I feel like if I try to say something, it’ll come out wrong, or I’ll freeze up in the moment. It’s hard to imagine feeling confident when I’m already so anxious about it.
therapist: It sounds like you’re feeling hesitant and unsure about how to approach this, and I can hear the underlying anxiety in your voice as you talk about freezing up or saying the wrong thing. Let’s start by practicing simple, calm responses in a safe space here—small, rehearsed phrases can help you feel more prepared and less overwhelmed when the moment comes. You don’t have to have it all figured out right now, and we can take it one step at a time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Okay, I can try practicing responses I guess... but what if my cousin just laughs or brushes me off? That would feel even worse than saying nothing. I've seen them do that to other people when they try to stand up for themselves, and it makes me feel like there's no point in trying.
therapist: It sounds like you’re feeling discouraged and worried about how your cousin might respond, and I can hear the frustration and concern in your voice as you talk about this. While it’s true they might react dismissively, the goal here isn’t to change their behavior—it’s to help you feel more grounded and confident in expressing yourself, even if their reaction isn’t ideal. Let’s focus on how you can respond in a way that feels true to you, regardless of how they react.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess focusing on how I feel instead of how they’ll react makes sense, but it’s still hard to imagine not caring about their response. I mean, their comments sting because it feels like they’re judging me, and I don’t know how to just brush that off. It’s like their words stick with me, even after the conversation is over.
therapist: It sounds like your cousin’s comments really linger with you, and I can hear the hurt and hesitation in your voice as you talk about how their words stick with you. It’s completely natural to feel judged and affected by their comments, but let’s explore how you can start to separate their judgments from your own sense of self-worth—because their words don’t define who you are or the value of your career choices. We can work on building a stronger, more compassionate perspective toward yourself, even when their comments feel sharp.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I like the idea of separating their judgments from my own worth, but it’s hard to actually do that. When they criticize my career, it feels like they’re saying I’m not good enough, and I can’t help but wonder if they’re right. It’s like their words dig into my own insecurities, and I don’t know how to stop that from happening.
therapist: It sounds like their comments are tapping into deeper insecurities, and I can hear the hurt and self-doubt in your voice as you talk about this. It’s so tough when criticism feels personal, but let’s explore how we can strengthen your confidence in your career choices and remind you of the reasons you’ve made them—because your worth isn’t defined by their opinions. We’ll work on building a perspective that helps you feel more secure in yourself, even when their words feel sharp.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess focusing on why I chose my career might help, but it’s hard to feel confident when I compare myself to others. My cousin’s comments always make me feel like I’m behind or not successful enough. I don’t know how to stop comparing myself, especially when it feels like everyone else is doing better than me.
therapist: It sounds like you’re feeling stuck in a cycle of comparison, and I can hear the frustration and self-doubt in your voice as you talk about this. Comparing ourselves to others can be so draining, but let’s focus on what success means to you personally—not what others think or say. Your career choices are yours for a reason, and we can work on reconnecting with those reasons to help you feel more grounded in your own journey.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I know I shouldn't compare myself, but it's hard when success seems so clearly defined in my family - big salary, fancy titles, all that. When I talk about my nonprofit work, it feels like they just see it as a hobby, not a "real career." I want to believe in my choices, but their judgment makes me second-guess everything.
therapist: It sounds like you’re feeling really torn between your family’s expectations and your own values, and I can hear the tension and defensiveness in your voice as you talk about this. Their dismissiveness toward your nonprofit work must feel so invalidating, especially when you’re doing something meaningful and purposeful. Let’s explore how you can reconnect with what truly matters to you in your career, rather than measuring yourself against a definition of success that doesn’t align with your passions.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I know I should focus on what matters to me, but it’s hard when I feel like I’m constantly defending my choices to my family. I want to believe in my work, but their comments make me feel like I’m not living up to their standards. It’s like no matter what I do, I’m always going to feel like I’m falling short.
therapist: It sounds like you’re feeling weighed down by the pressure to meet your family’s expectations, and I can hear the strain and vulnerability in your voice as you talk about this. It’s so hard to stay grounded in your own values when it feels like you’re constantly defending yourself, but let’s explore how you can shift your focus from their standards to what truly fulfills you. You don’t have to prove your worth to anyone—your work matters because it’s meaningful to you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
